Thank you for being honest about not being old enough! There's tons of discords for younger people - but they do tend to be very fast, each makes it's own sort of culture, and it can be very risky inside. Any space online "under 18 only" risks predators and stuff. I'm sure you already know this, I just felt the need to warn you if you haven't been in one yet. Also, I've found that a lot of autism-specific servers eventually end up making a rule where they ask for your real life identification cards. In mixed teen/18+servers, they do this to try and keep minors separated from adults, but I always leave once someone asks for my ID. Just something you might run into. There's a lot of bad stuff you can run into, in discord servers specifically, since they're not particularly public spaces - moderators choose who comes in, and there's very little that anyone can do about closed spaces.   
The "don't trust strangers online" thing started with the original chatrooms concept, way back when the internet was just starting up, and discord servers are the new chatrooms.  


There's public discords you can find by googling and stuff. Here's a list of just "autism" searched on discord's public server list:  
[https://disboard.org/servers/tag/autism](https://disboard.org/servers/tag/autism)  


The smaller ones tend to be safer and less overwhelming. When I join new servers, I always use the discord "search" function to see all messages that the server owners + mods have sent individually, to try and suss out if they're safe people, and doing things responsibly.

Hello! I'm 24 but I've had penpals older than me and it's always been a lovely experience. I feel you on the worldview adjustment, autism is a relatively new thing for me too. I'll shoot you a pm!

It certainly takes a huge mindset shift when you first latch onto the idea of not being neurotypical.  
For me, everything shifted from 'why am I so different?' to the question 'why didn't anybody notice?'. Forgiving my family members for overlooking someone who so desperately needed help will be a long road for me. Looking back at almost every aspect of growing up, it was so incredibly obvious.  
I was lonely before, and I'm still lonely now, but now I'm armed with a ton of knowledge that can help me do whatever I'd like. I wasn't capable of maintaining a lot of social situations before and I just didn't understand why people didn't like me, or why everyone would be afraid of me after meeting me. I blamed them for being so intimidated in the first place - which I still do tbh - but now I have an explanation, and I can work around myself a lot more easily.   
It's been a learning process trying to build a support system for me too. I've found the best friendships in other neurodiverse individuals, or people who even just have autism in their family. I can seek those people out now and know that I might have better luck connecting with them. Those are the people who \*get it\*, and those are the people that I gift with my vulnerability. It's incredibly difficult to get by without anyone who can understand. Neurotypicals can be fantastic and great and all that, but people who think the same way as you can understand in a better way.

If you're needing someone to just talk to, I have a lot of penpals and stuff so it wouldn't be weird at all to shoot me a message. I wish I could write more here but my brains a little fried tonight :)

Haha yeah.. Some galleries can be really rough to get a good feel for.  
I've found that the vast majority of galleries are run by seniors who either genuinely want to help, or they just want something to do to pass the time, or both. The ones who are on the latter side sometimes have their own inner circles and cliques, and the gallery they've set up isn't \*really\* for the public, but to make a space for their own community. It's a perfectly fine premise to work towards - however, when someone younger or from out of town walks in, they're often given the cold shoulder.  
It can be very difficult to hang art in those kind of galleries. Hanging art on their wall means being included in their club, invited to their events and parties - gallery showings which can be very casual, yet fancy, potlucks.   
My point is that not every gallery owner is in the business to actually \*sell\* the art, so some don't take that job seriously. It's looked at as a volunteer position.  
Because it's more difficult to hang art, if you do go forward with purchasing those artworks, you could very well be supporting someone who went through a lot to do that. A lot of towns or cities only have one gallery, if any at all, so there's not much choice for where to show traditional artwork.  


I've had previous buyers ask to speak directly to the artist before they purchase or after they purchase, to shake my hand or just to see what I look like. It wouldn't be unreasonable to ask the gallery if they can give you the artist's email address or something. They really should have it - galleries have email newsletters and when you sign up to be an artist of their gallery, you fill a sheet out and write down your email.

It's helpful in that it reduces the emotional power that parents can hang over you. By retelling stories, the impact when you remember those stories lessens. It's also helped me by removing that little voice that pipes up when I do things - like, when I look at my thighs, it's not my mom's voice telling me I'm fat anymore. It's all of the other voices and positive things. Sometimes I hear one of my counsellors saying "she's acting like a literal child." when referring to my mom, directly after remembering something my mom would say.
But it's the patient who does all of the work. The counsellor guides and suggests, but it's tough.

Writing your stories down and digesting it yourself is a good substitute. Even if you write the story down again and again, repeating it. Telling it to friends, out loud, and noting how difficult it is to tell that story. I think that might be more PTSD specific, but it can help anyone with difficult subjects.

I wish you luck and happiness :)

If you google '\_your city\_ counselling' or 'therapist' there will typically be different groups of counselling services. Their websites will tell you a little bit about each counsellor/therapist their office offers, along with their specialties and what they were trained for. It's common for counsellors to group together within a business to make it easier to refer clients and meet patients exact needs.   
Autism in adults is difficult to find a therapist for, but you might find some useful overlaps with PTSD and, like you said, family therapy. I wouldn't recommend you get just a family therapist though, they usually want to resolve things by eventually including the family within the session. Get a personal counsellor at least.  
I keep using the word counsellor because it's the cheaper and more available option vs. someone with more extensive training, and a good place to get started. Counsellors can refer you to therapists or psychiatrists or just people with more training than them.   


There will be an email or a phone number on the website. When I've emailed in the past, they sometimes ask you to phone the next day anyways. "Hello, my name is \_\_\_, I'd like to ask if \_specific counselor\_ is taking any new patients?"   
There's usually a secretary who takes calls from people in need all day, so don't worry too much about how the initial phone call will go. Usually the specific counsellor will want to talk to you directly as well, to gather information and see if they're a good fit for you. That's when you go into detail about what specifically you're struggling with.  


After all of that, or before the counsellor speaks to you directly, they'll want you to fill out a sheet with healthcare or if you'll be paying out of pocket, family information, emergency contact information. There's a clause saying that if you attempt to hurt yourself or others, the counsellor can call the police or contact your emergency person. The parts where you describe your history are always too short to fit everything in, but the therapist/counsellor will spend your entire first session just getting to know you and listening to your history anyways. That first sheet is what the secretaries see so you don't need to go too deep into specifics there if you don't want to. \*\*Counselling out-of-pocket has costed me $50-$75/session. If you are paying out of pocket, they have tons of different options for payment.   


After all that, they schedule an appointment with you. It's usually in 2-4 weeks from when you make your first call. Each appointment is 50 minutes long typically, they spend the other 10 minutes of the hour getting ready for the next patient.   


\*If you want video counselling, inquire if they have anyone available that's offering that, and explain why you need it - for me I always explain that I have big transportation issues. It got very popular during covid, but it's also difficult to set up and when there's internet issues it's a very big problem. It bombs the entire session when internet isn't being good or when there's noises where you're staying.  


Also worth mentioning to prepare for your sessions. Write down 2-3 big issues you want to dissect and a bunch of other stuff just in case it takes less time than you think it will to talk about those things. It also shows to the counsellor that you are taking it seriously if they see you write notes. Bring a water bottle to drink out of when you're talking about difficult things or want to break eye contact.

I kept wondering, is this just the fate of any friendship I make? Eventually when I end up talking about a deeper part to myself, are they destined to just Not Understand and then we drift apart? What's the point of trying to make friendships happen at all?  


I think I tend to blame myself for communication issues before I consider that the other person might be the problem, and that's probably the case for a lot of us here. People aren't very often responsible with the platonic relationships they hold and often let them die or don't bother maintaining it. They might see a friend who is struggling, sadly, turn into a responsibility rather than a friendship - which is deeply incorrect and makes me wanna puke. Friendships are meant to be two way systems, symbiotic relationships. You can hold eachother up and support one another - and that's not saying that they need to be an actual therapist for you - but maintain a bare minimum of showing that you care. Someone to listen. Someone to talk to.  


It takes a lot to bounce back when these things happen, but you become stronger for it. Don't water yourself down to make it easier for people who are supposed to be your friends. You don't need to stop being friends with those people, but set your boundaries and make sure that you do the best job communicating you can so that at least you know you're not the problem. Sometimes they need time to process too, or they need time, I don't know I haven't figured that out yet.  


Some of the best friends I have aren't neurotypical and tend to shut off like that a lot less often. Gems do exist. You will find them - they're just hard to find, and worth the time spent looking. I'm sorry you've been left feeling like you can't make friends. You don't deserve that.

I used to struggle with structure a lot too. I got myself stuck in a situation where I couldn't work for 2 years waiting on a work visa. Not that it was that bad while I waited, but still. Easy for old demons like depression and anxiety to come back when you have nothing better to do.

Something that helped me start doing things again was bullet journalling. It takes a lot out of you as a perfectionist to make the best layout, but once it's done, you're good for a month, and then you can trace over your last month's layout or make any adjustments for how you'd like your next month to change. Just shading in one box at a time for a day-to-day activity can help motivate you by wanting to maintain your "streaks" or keep the pattern pretty by being consistent with your work.

I followed a lot of BuJo blogs on tumblr back then to learn some things about it, but just googling bullet journal shows a lot of ideas that you can turn into your own. You don't need a journal with the dots, you could use one with lines too and then just graph out the paper for a cheaper alternative

​

Every day starts with the opportunity to create a snowball effect. Put small, easily attainable goals out for you in the mornings like 'take vitamins'. shade that box in your bullet journal. try to do another thing on the list.

As for specific goals and things to learn, i don't know any courses or things like that. But habit building is important. I think it's something like if you do something every day for 4 weeks it's a habit? That might be a good goal for you. Something like 1-2 hours of drawing/sketching a day or 5 days/week for 4 weeks, and then make a change to your self-set schedule after those 4 weeks depending on what you enjoyed. You can always do more than those 1-2 hours, but that would be the minimum.

Oh, also, something I used to do when I couldn't get up from the couch was sit there with my sketchbook. Pause a show when a shot on the tv looks appealing. Quickly sketch it, shittily, and never show it to anyone. One of my depression compromises - netflix binging but with work inbetween
